settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What it is
There are 26 bones in the foot and each joint between them has a range it should move through. Mobilisation is hands-on work to restore movement where a joint has become restricted.
People whose assessment shows a joint is not moving as it should, and that the restriction is changing how load passes through the foot.
Where it is available

image.alt: A podiatrist mobilising a patient’s foot by hand

settings.editor: In detail
The foot has 26 bones and two sesamoids. Joints can become stiff or partly dislocated (subluxed), which limits how well the foot moves.

image.alt: A practitioner mobilising the joints of a foot

settings.editor: 01
Cuboid syndrome: a bone on the outer side of the foot partly dislocates, often after an ankle sprain or with a foot that rolls in too far.
02

• Increase how far the joint moves
  • Reduce joint swelling
  • Restore normal muscle tone
  • Stretch tight tissue and break down adhesions
03
Mobilisation works through the foot, ankle, knee and hip joints. It is best used alongside orthotics and exercises.
04
Past fractures or stress fractures, a history of blood clots (DVT), fresh sprains and inflammation, severe osteoporosis or infection. Your podiatrist checks these first.
How it works here
Foot Mobilisation is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes which joints are restricted and whether that restriction is relevant to your pain.
02
The joint is mobilised by hand, working through its range rather than forcing it.
03
Mobilisation is usually paired with exercises or orthotic therapy so the range gained is kept.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What it is
Strapping applies tape to change how load passes through the foot, taking it off the tissue that is painful while that tissue settles.

People who need support straight away, and people for whom strapping is a test: if taping the foot a certain way relieves the pain, that tells us something useful about what an orthotic would need to do.
Where it is available

image.alt: Therapeutic strapping being applied to a patient’s foot

settings.editor: In detail
Strapping stimulates the nerve endings in the skin that sense pressure and position, improving how the body senses and controls the foot.

image.alt: Strapping tape applied around the foot and ankle

settings.editor: Four strapping techniques
Arch and heel
A figure-8 under the foot for plantar fasciitis, heel spurs and Sever’s disease.
Ankle
Supports ankle stability.
Knee
For knee pain around the kneecap.
Teenage knee
For pain at the growth area below the kneecap.
01
Strapping can protect against injury or give short-term support while other treatment takes effect.
02
How your foot responds to strapping helps show how much correction an orthotic will need.
03
For a foot that rolls in, the tape starts on the outer side to pull against it. For a foot that rolls out, it starts on the inner side.
How it works here
Foot Strapping is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes which tissue is overloaded and which direction needs supporting.
02
Tape is applied to offload that tissue. You will usually know within a day or two whether it has helped.
03
Strapping is short-term by design. Where it works, it often points towards orthotic therapy as the longer-term answer.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• A feeling of standing on a pebble or a fold in your sock
  • Burning or tingling that runs into the toes
  • Numbness in the toes
  • Relief when you take your shoe off and rub the foot
  • Worse in narrow or firm-soled shoes

The forefoot takes the highest pressure of any part of the foot at push-off. Pain there usually means pressure is concentrating where it should be spread — through foot alignment, footwear width, or the way load moves across the ball of the foot.

image.alt: Diagram of Morton’s neuroma between the metatarsals

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of Morton’s neuroma between the metatarsals</figcaption>
In detail
Pain in the ball of the foot falls into two main types. They feel different and have different causes.

image.alt: Diagram of metatarsalgia, pain across the ball of the foot

settings.editor: Two main types
General, burning
Pain spread across the ball of the foot. As a rolled-in foot lengthens, it creates shearing forces on the long bones’ heads and loses the arch across the forefoot.
Localised, nerve
A swelling of the nerve that runs between the metatarsals, the long bones of the foot — usually between the 2nd/3rd or 3rd/4th toes.
01

settings.title: How a neuroma changes over time

settings.editor: It starts as localised pain, then numbness, tingling or pins and needles into the toes. Over time the body forms scar tissue around the nerve to protect it.
02

settings.title: Why it needs a proper look

settings.editor: A cyst between the toes, bursitis or a torn plantar plate can feel similar. Telling them apart is part of the assessment.
03
Orthotics with a metatarsal dome, which supports the arch across the forefoot, dry needling, foot mobilisation and massage.
How we diagnose it
Forefoot Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess where pressure is concentrating across the forefoot as you walk.
02
We work out whether the problem is mechanical, footwear, or both, and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is aimed at redistributing that pressure rather than only settling the symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

Dr Abbie NajjarinePrincipal Podiatrist · Owner & Director Dr Abdalla Attar-HamouiPodiatrist Dr Elissa AllPodiatrist Dr Yousef NajjarinePodiatrist Dr Mohemed Al-HeyouryPodiatrist Dr Abbie NajjarinePrincipal Podiatrist · Owner & Director Dr Abdalla Attar-HamouiPodiatrist Dr Elissa AllPodiatrist

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Sharp pain under the heel with the first steps out of bed
  • Pain that eases as you warm up, then returns after sitting
  • Tenderness when you press the inside of the heel
  • Worse after a long day standing, or after exercise rather than during it

Most heel pain comes from pronation — the foot rolling in too far. As the arch drops, the foot lengthens and the plantar fascia is elongated, and that repeated stretching causes micro-tears at the base of the heel, where the fascia attaches. A heel spur seen on an X-ray is frequently a result of that loading rather than the cause of the pain.

image.alt: Diagram of a heel spur and the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of a heel spur and the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia</figcaption>
In detail
Most heel pain comes from the thick band of tissue under the foot (the plantar fascia) pulling where it attaches to the heel bone. Where on the heel it hurts is a clue to how your foot is moving.

image.alt: A hand holding a painful heel

settings.editor: Where it hurts points to why
Foot rolls in
Linked with the foot rolling inwards too far (over-pronation), which stretches the inner edge of the fascia.
Rolls out, then in
The foot lands on its outer edge, then rolls in. The heel becomes a pivot point for both movements.
Foot rolls out
Linked with the foot rolling outwards (supination), loading the outer attachment.
01

settings.title: Why the first steps hurt most

settings.editor: People often describe it as a hot, sharp pain through the heel when they get out of bed, taking 5–10 minutes to ease. It returns after sitting, and burns after a long day standing.
02

• Plantar fasciitis: repeated strain causes tiny tears and inflammation at the attachment.
  • Plantarfasciosis: over time the tissue thickens and scars, often without inflammation. It can be seen on ultrasound and is harder to treat the longer it is left.
  • Heel spur: a bony growth that forms as the body compensates. The pain feels the same.
03

Two people can both be told they have plantar fasciitis for opposite reasons: one whose longer leg rolls in to level up with the shorter one, another whose foot rolls out. The treatment is different for each, which is why the assessment comes first.
04
Orthotics with additions, strapping, massage and foot adjustments, shockwave, dry needling and injection therapy, each aimed at the area that hurts.
How we diagnose it
Heel Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess how you stand, walk and load rather than only pressing the sore spot, because the heel is usually where the pain shows up and not where it starts.
02
We identify what is overloading the tissue — alignment, footwear, activity, or the way the leg above the foot is working — and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is then prescribed against that finding, which is why two people with the same heel pain can leave with different plans.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Pain along the edge of the nail, usually the big toe
  • Redness or swelling of the skin beside the nail
  • Tender to pressure from shoes or bedsheets
  • Keeps returning after it seems to settle

Ingrown nails come from the shape of the nail, how it has been cut, pressure from footwear, or the way the toe loads when you walk. A nail that keeps becoming ingrown usually has a reason behind it rather than being bad luck.

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Pain around or under the kneecap
  • Worse on stairs, hills or after sitting for a while
  • Aching after activity rather than from a specific injury
  • One knee consistently worse than the other

The knee sits between the hip and the foot and is affected by both. Where the foot rolls in or out more than it should, the knee has to absorb that difference on every step — which is why knee pain with no injury behind it is often a lower limb alignment problem.

image.alt: Pain highlighted at the knee joint

settings.editor: <figcaption>Pain highlighted at the knee joint</figcaption>
In detail
Knee pain without an injury often starts at the foot. There are three areas of the knee, each linked to a different foot movement.

image.alt: Pain highlighted at the knee joint

settings.editor: Which part of the knee
Foot rolls in
For every degree the foot rolls in, the shin turns in by about the same amount, straining the inner knee ligament. The hip muscles tighten to compensate.
Rolls out, then in
The shin turns out, then suddenly in, twisting the knee so the kneecap tracks from side to side.
Foot rolls out
Rolling out through the whole step strains the outer knee ligament and can contribute to ITB syndrome.
01

A tender lump just below the kneecap, most often in active teenagers aged about 13–17 and more often boys. The kneecap tendon pulls on the growing area of the shin bone, and a twist in the leg can add to that pull.
02

settings.title: Why the hips come into it

settings.editor: When the shin is twisted, the hip muscles tighten to straighten the leg up. The knee is caught between the two, which is why the assessment includes the hips.
03
Orthotics, knee taping, dry needling, strengthening and stretching, mobilisation, shockwave and injection therapy.
How we diagnose it
Knee Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess alignment from the feet up rather than starting at the knee, because the knee is often where the pain shows up and not where it starts.
02
We identify what is changing the load at the knee and explain what we found.
03
Treatment addresses that cause. Where the foot is driving it, treating the foot is what changes the knee.
